title: Part 1, Chapter 18
paragraphs: In which is related the conversation Sancho Panza held with his master, Don Quixote, and other adventures worth relating

Sancho reached his master so limp and faint that he could not urge on his beast. When Don Quixote saw the state he was in, he said, "I have now come to the conclusion, good Sancho, that this castle or inn is beyond a doubt enchanted; for those who so atrociously amused themselves with you — what can they be but phantoms or beings of another world? I take this as confirmed by having noticed that when I was at the wall of the yard witnessing the acts of your sad tragedy, it was out of my power to climb up onto it, nor could I even dismount from Rocinante, because they no doubt had me enchanted. I swear to you by the faith of what I am, that if I had been able to climb up or dismount, I would have avenged you in such a way that those braggart thieves would have remembered their freak forever, even though in doing so I should have broken the laws of chivalry, which, as I have often told you, do not permit a knight to lay hands on one who is not, except in case of urgent and great necessity in defence of his own life and person."

"I would have avenged myself too if I could," said Sancho, "whether I had been dubbed knight or not — but I could not. Though for my part I am convinced those who amused themselves with me were not phantoms or enchanted men, as your worship says, but men of flesh and bone like ourselves. They all had names — I heard them call each other when they were tossing me; one was called Pedro Martinez, another Tenorio Hernandez, and the innkeeper, I heard, was called Juan Palomeque the Left-handed. So, señor, your not being able to leap over the wall of the yard or dismount from your horse was due to something other than enchantments. What I make of all this clearly is that the adventures we go seeking will in the end lead us into such misadventures that we won't know which is our right foot; and the best and wisest thing, in my small judgement, would be for us to return home, now that it is harvest time, and attend to our business, and give over wandering from Zeca to Mecca and from pail to bucket, as the saying is."

"How little you know about chivalry, Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "hold your peace and be patient. The day will come when you shall see with your own eyes what an honourable thing it is to wander in the pursuit of this calling. Tell me, what greater pleasure can there be in the world, or what delight can equal that of winning a battle and triumphing over one's enemy? None, beyond all doubt."

"Very likely," answered Sancho, "though I do not know it. All I know is that since we have been knights-errant — or since your worship has been one (for I have no right to count myself one of so honourable a number) — we have never won any battle except the one with the Biscayan, and even out of that your worship came with half an ear and half a helmet the less. From then till now it has been all cudgellings and more cudgellings, cuffs and more cuffs, I getting the blanketing on top of it all, and falling in with enchanted persons on whom I can't avenge myself so as to know what the delight of conquering an enemy is like, as your worship calls it."

"That is what vexes me, and what ought to vex you, Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "but from now on I will endeavour to have at hand some sword made with such craft that no kind of enchantment can take effect on him who carries it. It is even possible that fortune may procure for me the one that belonged to Amadis when he was called 'The Knight of the Burning Sword' — one of the best swords any knight in the world ever possessed; for besides having that virtue, it cut like a razor, and there was no armour, however strong and enchanted, that could resist it."

"Such is my luck," said Sancho, "that even if that happened and your worship found such a sword, it would, like the balsam, turn out to be useful and good only for dubbed knights, and as for the squires, they might sup sorrow."
"Fear not that, Sancho," said Don Quixote: "Heaven will deal better by you."

Talking like this, Don Quixote and his squire were going along when, on the road they were following, Don Quixote saw approaching them a large and thick cloud of dust; on seeing which he turned to Sancho and said:

"This is the day, Sancho, on which will be seen the boon my fortune is reserving for me; this, I say, is the day on which, as much as on any other, the might of my arm will be displayed, and on which I shall do deeds that shall remain written in the book of fame for all ages to come. Do you see that cloud of dust rising yonder? Well then, it is being churned up by a vast army composed of various and countless nations marching there."
"In that case there must be two," said Sancho, "for on the opposite side here there rises just such another cloud of dust."

Don Quixote turned to look and found it was true. Rejoicing greatly, he concluded that they were two armies about to engage and clash in the middle of that broad plain; for at all times and seasons his imagination was full of the battles, enchantments, adventures, crazy feats, loves, and defiances recorded in the books of chivalry, and everything he said, thought, or did had reference to such things. Now the cloud of dust he had seen was raised by two great droves of sheep coming along the same road in opposite directions, which, because of the dust, did not become visible until they drew near. But Don Quixote insisted so positively that they were armies that Sancho was led to believe it, and said, "Well, what are we to do, señor?"

"What?" said Don Quixote; "give aid and assistance to the weak and those in need. You must know, Sancho, that the army coming towards us is led and commanded by the mighty emperor Alifanfaron, lord of the great island of Trapobana; the other that marches behind me is that of his enemy, the king of the Garamantas, Pentapolin of the Bare Arm — so called because he always goes into battle with his right arm bare."
"But why are these two lords such enemies?"

"They are at enmity," replied Don Quixote, "because this Alifanfaron is a furious pagan and is in love with the daughter of Pentapolin, who is a very beautiful and gracious lady, and a Christian; and her father refuses to give her to the pagan king unless he first abandons the religion of his false prophet Mahomet and adopts his own."
"By my beard," said Sancho, "Pentapolin is quite right, and I'll help him all I can."
"In that you will do what is your duty, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "for to engage in battles of this sort there is no requirement of being a dubbed knight."

"That I can well understand," answered Sancho; "but where shall we put this ass to be sure of finding him again after the fray is over? Because I don't believe it has been the custom so far to go into battle on a beast of this kind."

"That is true," said Don Quixote, "and the best thing you can do with him is to leave him to his fate, whether he be lost or not, for we shall have so many horses when we come out victorious that even Rocinante runs a risk of being exchanged for another. But pay attention and observe, for I want to give you some account of the chief knights in these two armies; and so that you may see and mark them better, let us withdraw to that hillock rising yonder, from which both armies can be seen."

They did so, and placed themselves on a rising ground from which the two droves that Don Quixote made armies of might have been plainly seen, if the clouds of dust they raised had not obscured and blinded the sight. Nevertheless, seeing in his imagination what he did not see and what did not exist, he began in a loud voice:

"That knight you see yonder in yellow armour, who bears on his shield a lion crowned crouching at the feet of a damsel, is the valiant Laurcalco, lord of the Silver Bridge; that one in armour with flowers of gold, who bears on his shield three crowns argent on an azure field, is the dreaded Micocolembo, grand duke of Quirocia; that other of giant frame, on his right hand, is the ever-dauntless Brandabarbaran de Boliche, lord of the three Arabias, who for armour wears that serpent skin and has for shield a gate which, according to tradition, is one of those of the temple Samson brought to the ground when by his death he revenged himself on his enemies. But turn your eyes to the other side and you shall see, in the front and vanguard of this other army, the ever-victorious and never-vanquished Timonel of Carcajona, prince of New Biscay, who comes in armour with arms quartered azure, vert, white, and yellow, and bears on his shield a cat or on a field tawny with a motto that says _Miau_, which is the beginning of the name of his lady, who according to report is the peerless Miaulina, daughter of the duke Alfeniquen of the Algarve. The other, who burdens and presses the loins of that powerful charger and bears arms white as snow and a shield blank and without any device, is a novice knight, a Frenchman by birth, Pierres Papin by name, lord of the baronies of Utrique. That other, who with iron-shod heels strikes the flanks of that nimble parti-coloured zebra, and for arms bears azure vair, is the mighty duke of Nerbia, Espartafilardo del Bosque, who bears for device on his shield an asparagus plant with a motto in Castilian that says, _'Rastrea mi suerte'_." And so he went on naming a great many knights of one squadron or the other out of his imagination, and to all he assigned off the cuff their arms, colours, devices, and mottoes, carried away by the illusions of his unheard-of mania. Without a pause, he continued, "The people of various nations compose this squadron in front: here are those who drink from the sweet waters of the famous Xanthus; those who scour the wooded Massilian plains; those who sift the pure fine gold of Arabia Felix; those who enjoy the famed cool banks of the crystal Thermodon; those who in many and various ways divert the streams of the golden Pactolus; the Numidians, faithless in their promises; the Persians renowned in archery; the Parthians and the Medes who fight as they fly; the Arabs who are forever shifting their dwellings; the Scythians as cruel as they are fair; the Ethiopians with pierced lips; and an infinity of other nations whose features I recognise, though I cannot recall their names. In this other squadron come those who drink the crystal streams of the olive-bearing Betis; those who smooth their faces with the water of the ever-rich and golden Tagus; those who rejoice in the fertilising flow of the divine Genil; those who roam the Tartesian plains abounding in pasture; those who take their pleasure in the Elysian meadows of Jerez; the rich Manchegans crowned with ruddy ears of corn; the wearers of iron, old relics of the Gothic race; those who bathe in the Pisuerga renowned for its gentle current; those who feed their herds along the spreading pastures of the winding Guadiana, famed for its hidden course; those who tremble with the cold of the pine-clad Pyrenees or the dazzling snows of the lofty Apennine — in a word, as many as all Europe includes and contains."

Good God! What a number of countries and nations he named! Giving to each its proper attributes with marvellous readiness — brimful and saturated with what he had read in his lying books! Sancho Panza hung on his words without speaking, and from time to time turned to try if he could see the knights and giants his master was describing; and as he could not make out a single one of them he said:
"Señor, devil take it if there's a sign of any man you talk of, knight or giant, in the whole thing; maybe it's all enchantment, like the phantoms last night."
"How can you say that!" answered Don Quixote; "don't you hear the neighing of the steeds, the braying of the trumpets, the roll of the drums?"
"I hear nothing but a great bleating of ewes and sheep," said Sancho; which was true, for by this time the two flocks had come close.

"The fear you are in, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "prevents you from seeing or hearing correctly, for one of the effects of fear is to derange the senses and make things appear different from what they are. If you are in such fear, withdraw to one side and leave me to myself, for alone I am enough to bring victory to the side I give my aid to." So saying, he gave Rocinante the spur, and putting his lance in rest, shot down the slope like a thunderbolt. Sancho shouted after him, "Come back, Señor Don Quixote; I vow to God they are sheep and ewes you are charging! Come back! Unlucky the father that begot me! What madness is this? Look, there is no giant, nor knight, nor cats, nor arms, nor shields quartered or whole, nor vair azure or bedevilled. What are you doing? Sinner that I am before God!" But not for all these entreaties did Don Quixote turn back; on the contrary, he went on shouting, "Ho, knights, you who follow and fight under the banners of the valiant emperor Pentapolin of the Bare Arm, follow me all of you; you shall see how easily I shall give him his revenge over his enemy Alifanfaron of the Trapobana."

So saying, he dashed into the middle of the squadron of ewes, and began to spear them with as much spirit and intrepidity as if he were transfixing mortal enemies in earnest. The shepherds and drovers accompanying the flock shouted at him to stop; seeing it was no use, they ungirt their slings and began to salute his ears with stones as big as a fist. Don Quixote paid no heed to the stones, but, letting drive right and left, kept saying:

"Where are you, proud Alifanfaron? Come before me; I am a single knight who wants to test your prowess hand to hand, and make you yield your life as a penalty for the wrong you do to the valiant Pentapolin Garamanta." Here came a sugar-plum from the brook that struck him on the side and buried a couple of ribs in his body. Feeling himself so smitten, he imagined himself slain or badly wounded for certain, and remembering his liquor he drew out his flask, put it to his mouth, and began to pour the contents into his stomach; but before he had managed to swallow what seemed to him enough, another almond came that struck him on the hand and on the flask so fairly that it smashed the flask to pieces, knocking three or four teeth and grinders out of his mouth in the process, and badly crushing two fingers of his hand. Such was the force of the first blow and of the second that the poor knight, in spite of himself, came down backwards off his horse. The shepherds came up, and felt sure they had killed him; so in all haste they collected their flock together, took up the dead beasts — of which there were more than seven — and made off without waiting to find out anything further.

All this time Sancho stood on the hill watching the crazy feats his master was performing, and tearing his beard and cursing the hour and occasion when fortune had made him acquainted with him. Seeing him then brought to the ground, and that the shepherds had taken themselves off, he ran to him and found him in a very bad way, though not unconscious; and said:
"Didn't I tell you to come back, Señor Don Quixote, and that what you were going to attack were not armies but droves of sheep?"

"That's how that thief of a sage, my enemy, can alter and falsify things," answered Don Quixote; "you must know, Sancho, that it is a very easy matter for people of his sort to make us believe whatever they choose; and this malignant being who persecutes me, envious of the glory he knew I was to win in this battle, has turned the enemy squadrons into droves of sheep. At any rate, do this much, I beg of you, Sancho — to undeceive yourself, and see that what I say is true: mount your ass and follow them quietly, and you'll see that when they have gone some little way from here they will return to their original shape and, ceasing to be sheep, become men in all respects as I described them to you at first. But don't go just yet, for I need your help and assistance. Come here, and see how many of my teeth and grinders are missing, for I feel as if there isn't one left in my mouth."

Sancho came so close that he almost put his eyes into his mouth; and just at that moment the balsam was acting on Don Quixote's stomach, so at the very instant when Sancho came to examine his mouth, he discharged all its contents with more force than a musket, full into the beard of the compassionate squire.

"Holy Mary!" cried Sancho, "what is this that has happened to me? Clearly this sinner is mortally wounded, since he vomits blood from his mouth"; but considering the matter a little more closely, he perceived by the colour, taste, and smell that it was not blood but the balsam from the flask he had seen him drink. And he was taken with such a loathing that his stomach turned, and he vomited up his insides over his very master, and both were left in a precious state. Sancho ran to his ass to get something out of his saddlebags to clean himself and relieve his master; but not finding them, he nearly took leave of his senses, cursed himself anew, and resolved in his heart to quit his master and return home, even if he forfeited the wages of his service and all hopes of the promised island.

Don Quixote now rose, and putting his left hand to his mouth to keep his teeth from falling out altogether, with the other he laid hold of Rocinante's bridle — the horse had never stirred from his master's side, so loyal and well-behaved was he — and went over to where the squire stood leaning over his ass with his hand to his cheek, like a man in deep dejection. Seeing him in this mood, looking so sad, Don Quixote said:

"Bear in mind, Sancho, that one man is no more than another, unless he does more than another. All these tempests that fall upon us are signs that fair weather is coming shortly, and that things will go well with us, for it is impossible for good or evil to last forever; and so it follows that, the evil having lasted long, the good must be now close at hand. So you must not distress yourself at the misfortunes that happen to me, since you have no share in them."

"How have I not?" replied Sancho. "Was the one they blanketed yesterday perhaps anyone other than my father's son? And the saddlebags that are missing today with all my treasures — did they belong to anyone but me?"
"What! The saddlebags are missing, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.
"Yes, they are missing," answered Sancho.
"In that case we have nothing to eat today," replied Don Quixote.

"It would be so," answered Sancho, "if there were none of those herbs your worship says you know about in these meadows — the ones with which knights-errant as unlucky as your worship are accustomed to make up for such shortcomings."

"For all that," answered Don Quixote, "I would rather have right now a quarter of bread, or a loaf and a couple of pilchards' heads, than all the herbs described by Dioscorides, even with Doctor Laguna's notes. Nevertheless, Sancho the Good, mount your beast and come along with me; God, who provides for all things, will not fail us — especially when we are so active in his service as we are — since he fails not the midges of the air, nor the grubs of the earth, nor the tadpoles of the water, and is so merciful that he maketh his sun to rise on the good and on the evil, and sendeth rain on the unjust and on the just."
"Your worship would make a better preacher than knight-errant," said Sancho.

"Knights-errant knew and ought to know everything, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "for there were knights-errant in former times as well qualified to deliver a sermon or discourse in the middle of an encampment as if they had taken a degree at the University of Paris; whereby we may see that the lance has never blunted the pen, nor the pen the lance."

"Well, be it as your worship says," replied Sancho; "let us be off now and find some place of shelter for the night, and God grant it may be somewhere where there are no blankets, nor blanketeers, nor phantoms, nor enchanted Moors; for if there are, may the devil take the whole concern."

"Ask that of God, my son," said Don Quixote; "and lead on wherever you like, for this time I leave our lodging to your choice. But reach me your hand, and feel with your finger, and tell me how many teeth and grinders are missing from this right side of my upper jaw, for that is where I feel the pain."
Sancho put in his fingers, and feeling about, asked him, "How many grinders did your worship have on this side?"
"Four," replied Don Quixote, "besides the back-tooth, all whole and quite sound."
"Mind what you are saying, señor."
"I say four, if not five," answered Don Quixote, "for never in my life have I had a tooth or grinder drawn, nor has any fallen out or been destroyed by decay or rheum."
"Well, then," said Sancho, "on this lower side your worship has no more than two grinders and a half, and on the upper neither a half nor any at all — it's all as smooth as the palm of my hand."

"Luckless that I am!" said Don Quixote, hearing the sad news his squire gave him. "I had rather they had stripped me of an arm, so long as it were not my sword-arm; for I tell you, Sancho, a mouth without teeth is like a mill without a millstone, and a tooth is much more to be prized than a diamond. But we who profess the austere order of chivalry are liable to all this. Mount, friend, and lead the way, and I will follow you at whatever pace you wish."

Sancho did as he was told, and proceeded in the direction in which he thought he might find shelter without leaving the high road, which was very much frequented there. As they went along at a slow pace — for the pain in Don Quixote's jaws kept him uneasy and not in the mood for speed — Sancho thought it well to amuse and divert him with talk of some kind, and among the things he said to him was what will be told in the following chapter.
